questions.q: Which compound does NOT give a yellow precipitate with I₂ and NaOH?
questions.explain: A positive iodoform test needs CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–. Pentan-3-one has ethyl groups on both sides of C=O, so it has no CH₃CO unit.

questions.q: Acetophenone is treated with Br₂ and aqueous NaOH. The products are:
questions.explain: In base the CH₃ group is fully brominated and then cleaved as ⁻CBr₃, giving bromoform and the carboxylate with one carbon fewer. Base-promoted halogenation cannot be stopped at the monobromo stage.

questions.q: For the base-promoted halogenation of acetone, rate = k[ketone][OH⁻]. Which conclusion follows?
options: Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ react at the same rate because enolate formation is rate-determining
Halogen attack on the enolate is the slow step
F₂ reacts fastest because it is the most reactive halogen
Cleavage of ⁻CX₃ is the slow step
questions.explain: The halogen does not appear in the rate law, so removal of the α-hydrogen by OH⁻ is the slow step and the rate is the same for Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. Fluorine is not used at all because hypofluorite is too unstable.

questions.q: Acetamide (CH₃CONH₂) is treated with Br₂ and aqueous NaOH. The organic product is:
questions.explain: A primary amide with Br₂/NaOH undergoes the Hofmann bromamide degradation to R–NH₂, not the haloform reaction; acetamide is listed among the iodoform-negative compounds. The trap is spotting CH₃CO– and writing a haloform.
